turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Describe the project that best shows mobile skills: users, problem, responsibility
card.heard: pick the project, who used it, problem, my responsibility
card.say: Good evening, and thanks for the introduction. The project I'd pick is the AI trip planner at KKday. It was used by travelers on our Android app, people booking tours and activities in many markets. Planning a trip by hand was slow: they worked out the budget, searched products one by one, then put the plan together. I was the technical lead for a five-person project. I designed the agent, connected it to our real product and order data, and built the core backend. My responsibility ended at the app side of the result display; the app team owned the rest of the Android screens. After launch, the system handled about 300,000 trip planning requests every day.
card.then: Next, I can explain how the plan is checked before users see it.

updates: The SSE parsing had to handle partial frames and reconnects without duplicating plan steps, and I capped concurrent planning sessions per user so one heavy request couldn't starve the shared model quota.
The streamed result had to stay readable while tokens arrived, so I rendered plan steps incrementally and kept the final order stable once the stream closed.
I also had to keep latency predictable under that load, so I set a per-request token budget and fell back to a cached partial plan when the model queue backed up.
The first day card shows up while the rest of the plan is still being made, and if a plan fails our checks, the app shows a safe fallback instead of a broken screen.
I also defined the error contract with the app team, so each failure type mapped to a specific user-facing message rather than a generic error.
I also set the retry policy for those streams: a dropped connection retries with the last received step index, so the user never sees a step twice or loses their place.

I also added a small server-side guard that rejects a planning request early if the user's saved budget or destination is missing, so the model isn't spent on a request that can't produce a usable plan.

The trade-off was that the early guard rejects some requests users could have completed by filling in the missing field later, so we surfaced a prompt to complete their profile instead of failing silently.
The part I'm proudest of is the streaming: users see day one right away instead of waiting for the whole plan.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said you designed the agent and built the core backend, but the app team owned the rest of the Android screens. Which exact pieces did you personally write versus what the team built?

card.problem: Describe the project that best shows mobile skills: users, problem, responsibility
card.heard: which exact pieces did you personally write
card.say: I wrote the agent design and the core backend myself. On Android, I wrote the code that reads the SSE stream of the trip plan. The app team built the other screens, like the product cards and the map. I also agreed the response format with them, so each day card and map point had a fixed shape.

updates: I also wrote the backend checks that validate each plan before it reaches the app.
The checks also cover the location limits, and when one fails the backend retries with the exact error before falling back to a safe default.
The retry loop is capped at two attempts, so a persistent failure returns the safe default rather than looping.
The main trade-off is latency: validating and retrying adds a short delay before the plan reaches the user, which I kept small by only re-requesting the failed part rather than the whole plan.

One more piece I should be clear about: the personalization data layer was mine too. It used search history, preferences, location and past purchases, and both trip planning and search recommendations sat on it.
The personalization layer also had to handle cold-start users with no history, so for those I fell back to location and popular items rather than leaving recommendations empty.
The cold-start fallback was deliberately coarse: it ignores any partial signal, so a user with only one or two interactions is treated the same as a brand-new one until enough history accumulates.
The day card rendering on Android was also mine, and it consumed the fixed response shape we agreed with the app team.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: On the Debon Securities release where you kept the old pages behind a switch, what risk were you willing to accept before shipping, who watched the data afterwards, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk or likely delay where the team disagreed: when, whom, options, who decided, what you finished
card.heard: Risk accepted, who watched the data, what signal to roll back
card.say: The risk I accepted was that the old pages still had their own bugs. My switch only covered my change, so I couldn't turn those off. I accepted it because the old pages were already live and stable for users. My change was the new part, so that was the part we could switch off. I watched the data myself, with QA. We looked at crash reports in Bugly and at back-button errors from users. The signal to roll back was simple. If crashes or back-button errors went up after the release, I'd turn my change off with the switch.
card.then: Next, I can say what I'd do differently if the old pages had failed too.

updates: I'd set a clear threshold: a small rise in back-button errors is fine, but a clear spike means we pause the rollout, and if the crash rate for the new flow doubles, I'd roll back the switch that day. I'd agree the numbers with QA before release, so nobody argues about them later.

I'd also watch the crash-free rate, not just the raw crash count. A small app has small numbers, so one bad device can look like a spike. So I'd compare the new flow against the old one over the same days. If the new flow was clearly worse, I'd pause the rollout first and roll back only if it stayed worse.
I'd also set a minimum sample size before acting, so a handful of sessions on a quiet day doesn't trigger a rollback.

I'd also check whether the crash is happening on a specific Android version or device model, since a spike concentrated on one device type usually points to a compatibility issue rather than a problem with the new flow itself.
One more thing I'd watch: ANRs, not just crashes. A back-button problem can freeze the app instead of crashing it. If it rose clearly above the old pages, I'd pause the rollout the same way.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the server writes the ledger entry and the idempotency record in the same transaction — walk me through that on the server: what exactly gets written, in what order, and how the lock on A's row fits in.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a saved contact, confirmed on a native screen, with the server ledger as the single source of truth", "Per-transfer and per-day limits for new recipients, with a second native confirmation above the limit, checked on the server"]
card.heard: walk through the server transaction for A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: The server starts one database transaction. First it locks A's row, so no other send can read A's balance at the same time. Then it checks the limits and the balance. Next it writes the debit for A and the credit for B, so A goes from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80. Last it writes the idempotency record with the client ID and the request details, and commits. If anything fails, the whole transaction rolls back, so there's no debit without its record. The amount travels as a Long in cents, never a floating-point number.

updates: The lock is released when the transaction commits or rolls back. I'd prove it with two phones sending at the same time, and the ledger should still show one debit. The amount travels as a Long in cents, never a floating-point number.

I'd also keep the lock short: no model calls or network calls inside the transaction. If the commit itself times out, the client doesn't know the result, so it retries with the same client ID and the server answers with the original status.

The lock is on A's row only, so B's row is free for other transfers. I'd also add a unique index on the client ID, so a second insert fails at the database level. That way the check doesn't depend on my code alone.
If two retries of the same client ID arrive at once, only one insert wins, and the other one reads the original record and returns its status.
